value.title: Intentional Action and Side-Effects in Ordinary Language

participants.population: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

Experiment 1.population: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

Experiment 2.population: People spending time in a Manhattan public park.

steps: Participants are randomly assigned to either a 'harm condition' or a 'help condition'.
Participants read a vignette (either about a corporate chairman or a military lieutenant) implementing a plan with a known side-effect that the agent claims not to care about.
Participants assess how much blame (in the harm condition) or praise (in the help condition) the agent deserves on a scale from 0 to 6.
Participants answer a categorical (Yes/No) question regarding whether the agent brought about the side-effect intentionally.

steps: Subjects are recruited and provided with a $10 show-up fee.

In the Social History treatment, subjects are provided with a report summarizing the results (amount sent, number of persons, average amount returned, and average profit) of the 32 pairs from the No History treatment.
Room A subjects decide how much of their $10 show-up fee to send to an anonymous counterpart in Room B.
The amount sent by Room A subjects is tripled by the experimenters.
Room B subjects receive the tripled amount and decide how much to send back to the person in Room A and how much to keep.

program.title: Testing the decoy effect to improve online survey participation: Evidence from a field experiment

source.title: Testing the decoy effect to improve online survey participation: Evidence from a field experiment
source.authors: Sandro T. Stoffel, Yining Sun, Yasemin Hirst, Christian von Wagner, Ivo Vlaev

studies.title: Field experiment on the decoy effect in survey participation

value.description: Respondents generally preferred close-ended questions over open-ended questions.
value.hypothesis: Open-ended questions would be perceived as less attractive than close-ended questions and therefore could function as an inferior decoy attribute.
value.raw_outcomes: Among N=210 preliminary questionnaire respondents: close-ended questions 61.4% (n~129), open-ended questions 7.9% (n~17), indifferent 30.7% (n~64). Exact counts NOT PROVIDED in paper.

value.description: Most respondents indicated they would not participate if remuneration were received only after four weeks.
value.hypothesis: Delayed remuneration would be perceived as less attractive than sooner remuneration and therefore could function as an inferior decoy attribute.
value.raw_outcomes: Among N=210 preliminary questionnaire respondents: Definitely not 1.0% (n~2), Probably not 85.1% (n~179), Probably yes 1.5% (n~3), Definitely yes 12.4% (n~26). Overall 86.1% would not respond if remuneration in four weeks.

nodes.title: Field experiment on the decoy effect in survey participation

value.description: Randomization produced similar groups on most sociodemographic variables, except ethnicity.
value.hypothesis: No explicit hypothesis; balance checks were used to compare control and decoy groups.

statistical_tests.claim: No age difference between control and decoy groups.
No gender difference between control and decoy groups.
Ethnicity differed between conditions; the decoy condition contained more White participants (67.7% vs 47.5%).
No religion difference between control and decoy groups at conventional significance levels.
No education difference between control and decoy groups.

value.description: The presence of the decoy option increased completion of the target survey.
value.hypothesis: Among those likely to take part in a survey, the presence of a decoy version of the same survey on the invitation will increase the chances of completing the target version.

raw_data.note: Table 2 / Table S3 reports decoy as 59.8%, but text, flow diagram, and participant-level data imply 57/102 = 55.9%

statistical_tests.claim: Target-survey completion was significantly higher in the decoy condition (55.9%) than in the control condition (32.7%).
statistical_tests.location: Main paper Results section 3.2.2 and Fig. 3

raw_data.note: As reported in Table 2, Model 1; Supplementary Table S3

statistical_tests.claim: In the unadjusted model, the decoy condition significantly increased the odds of completing the target survey relative to control.
statistical_tests.location: Main paper Table 2, Model 1; Supplementary Table S3

groundTruth.title: Testing the decoy effect to improve online survey participation: Evidence from a field experiment

preliminary_study_findings.description: Respondents generally preferred close-ended questions over open-ended questions.
preliminary_study_findings.hypothesis: Open-ended questions would be perceived as less attractive than close-ended questions and therefore could function as an inferior decoy attribute.
preliminary_study_findings.raw_outcomes: Among N=210 preliminary questionnaire respondents: close-ended questions 61.4% (n~129), open-ended questions 7.9% (n~17), indifferent 30.7% (n~64). Exact counts NOT PROVIDED in paper.

preliminary_study_findings.description: Most respondents indicated they would not participate if remuneration were received only after four weeks.
preliminary_study_findings.hypothesis: Delayed remuneration would be perceived as less attractive than sooner remuneration and therefore could function as an inferior decoy attribute.
preliminary_study_findings.raw_outcomes: Among N=210 preliminary questionnaire respondents: Definitely not 1.0% (n~2), Probably not 85.1% (n~179), Probably yes 1.5% (n~3), Definitely yes 12.4% (n~26). Overall 86.1% would not respond if remuneration in four weeks.

main_study.study_name: Field experiment on the decoy effect in survey participation

findings.description: Randomization produced similar groups on most sociodemographic variables, except ethnicity.
findings.hypothesis: No explicit hypothesis; balance checks were used to compare control and decoy groups.

statistical_tests.claim: No age difference between control and decoy groups.
No gender difference between control and decoy groups.
Ethnicity differed between conditions; the decoy condition contained more White participants (67.7% vs 47.5%).
No religion difference between control and decoy groups at conventional significance levels.
No education difference between control and decoy groups.

findings.description: The presence of the decoy option increased completion of the target survey.
findings.hypothesis: Among those likely to take part in a survey, the presence of a decoy version of the same survey on the invitation will increase the chances of completing the target version.
